title: Supporting students’ self‑regulated learning in online learning using artificial intelligence applications
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how university students perceive the use of artificial intelligence (AI) applications to support self-regulated learning (SRL) in online learning environments. The authors argue that SRL is essential for success in online learning, but many learners struggle to regulate cognition, metacognition, behavior, and motivation without strong instructor presence. The study specifically asks how students view AI support across different SRL phases and areas, and what pedagogical and psychological considerations they believe are necessary for these tools to be effective.

To explore these questions, the researchers used a qualitative speed-dating method with storyboards rather than deploying actual software. They developed 10 storyboarded AI application scenarios aligned with SRL strategies, including tools such as a plan organizer, pre-question generator, intelligent suggestions, AI analytics dashboard, AI agent for help-seeking, adaptive quiz, and AI reflection tool. Semi-structured interviews were then conducted with 16 university students, who reacted to the scenarios and discussed when, how, and whether they would use such AI supports in their online learning.

The population consisted of undergraduate students from 10 majors across four academic disciplines who had at least six months of experience with fully online learning. The participants were university students in South Korea, and the context was online higher education. The study did not test learning gains experimentally; instead, it examined student perceptions of potential usefulness, concerns, and design requirements for AI-supported SRL.

The main conclusions are that students generally perceived AI applications as useful for supporting metacognitive, cognitive, and behavioral regulation, especially for planning, monitoring progress, reviewing, and obtaining immediate help. However, they were less positive about AI applications aimed at motivational regulation, such as virtual humans or AI companions. The authors identify three major design considerations for effective AI-supported SRL: learner identity (acknowledging that learners differ and change over time), learner activeness (supporting agency rather than overdependence on AI), and learner position (recognizing that students are both autonomous learners and grade-dependent participants in institutional systems). The paper concludes that AI tools for online learning should be designed with these pedagogical and psychological factors in mind to better support human-AI symbiosis in education.

identified_tools.name: Adaptive Feedback System (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic AI-supported adaptive and feedback applications for supporting students' self-regulated learning in online learning, including planning, analytics, question answering, adaptive quizzing, reflection, and related scaffolds.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper used 10 storyboarded AI application scenarios (e.g., plan organizer, AI analytics, AI agent, adaptive quiz, AI reflection) in speed-dating interviews to explore university students' perceptions of how AI could support self-regulated learning; no actual tool was implemented or evaluated empirically for learning outcomes.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative exploratory design study using storyboard-based speed-dating interviews with 16 university students. It does not evaluate an implemented AI tool or test causal effects on student outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports perceived usefulness and design considerations rather than measured impacts on academic or behavioral outcomes. Impact is therefore unclear and not quantified.
